cards.explanation: The answer is lies and plunder. Nahum calls Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, "…full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey." Three phrases in one breath, and none of them are flattering, friends. You hear that and know right away this is not a city you'd want to be left alone in.

The answer is True. Nahum moves from the "Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear…" straight to "heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end…" This is a heavy part of the passage, friends. I think this one hurts.

The word is "betrays." Nahum says she "…betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft." Betrayal is the whole charge here, friends. She is doing this to the very ones she deals with.
The answer is "against." "Behold, I am against you," declares the LORD of Hosts. Notice how plain and short that is, friends. Everything that follows in this passage comes after those words.

The answer is the nations and kingdoms. The LORD says, "I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms." The audience is wide, not just the neighbors. Everyone watching sees it, bakers, and that is the point of the line.

The word is "grieve." All who see her "…will recoil from you and say, ‘Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?’…" Then the LORD asks, "Where can I find comforters for you?" Two questions, friends, and the verse leaves them as questions.
The answer is Cush and Egypt. Nahum says, "Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength…" Thebes was a city by the Nile, and she had real backing, friends. That makes her story hit harder.
The answer is False. Nahum says, "Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity." The water and the allies are named, friends, and still that is what he says. Nahum tells it plainly.

The answer is they cast lots. Nahum says, "They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains." Casting lots is how the enemy settled who got which person, friends. The text doesn't say more than that, so I won't either.

The answer is that strong walls and allies didn't save her. That's the point, friends. Nahum asks Nineveh, "Are you better than Thebes…" Thebes had the Nile around her and Cush, Egypt, Put and Libya behind her, and she still went into captivity. If it happened to her, Nineveh shouldn't count on her own strength.

The word is "refuge." Nahum says, "You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy." The city that was so loud earlier is looking for a place to hide, friends. That's quite a change.

The answer is that the figs fall into the eater's mouth. Nahum says, "All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater!" Shake the tree and the figs fall, bakers. That's how he pictures her fortresses.
The answer is True. Nahum says, "The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars." Gates are supposed to keep people out, friends. These are wide open.

The answer is that the fire will devour her. After telling her to strengthen her fortresses, Nahum says, "There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down…" All that brick work and she still ends up there, friends. Strengthening doesn't change what's coming.
The word is "strips." Nahum says, "The young locust strips the land and flies away." Strips is what the locust does, friends, and then it flies away.

The answer is they fly away. Nahum says the locusts "…settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where." He pictures her scribes the same way, friends. They look settled until the sun comes up.
The answer is False. Nahum says, "When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where." Nobody can say where they went, friends. They're simply gone.

The word is "scattered." Nahum says to the king of Assyria, "Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them." Scattered, with nobody to bring them together, friends. That's the king's problem.
The answer is they applaud his downfall. Nahum says, "All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall…" Nobody in this verse is quiet about it, friends. The news travels and the applause follows.

The answer is that they've all felt his constant cruelty. That's the reason Nahum gives. He says everyone applauds, "…for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?" He ends the whole book on that question, friends. Everyone has felt it.
